docs.text: Introduction # Have you ever looked up on a clear, moonless night and beheld the beauty of our home galaxy, the Milky Way, across the night sky? If you are able to do this from the comfort of your own backyard, you should consider yourself lucky. Due to light pollution, which plagues urban areas around the world, the majority of people cannot experience such luxury, and are forced to travel potentially hours away from home to catch a glimpse of the Milky Way. Electric lighting, first invented in the 19th century, is arguably one of the most important of the modern inventions, allowing us to extend our working hours past sunset and long into the night. However, with all of this artificial light at night, some of it will inevitably end up being scattered into the night sky and lost. This scattering of light into the night sky results in an unnatural brightening of the night sky, called skyglow. Also known as light pollution, it affects not only astronomical observations, but also the quality of the lives of both people and wildlife. Figure 1: The effect of light pollution on the night sky. (drag to compare images) Image source: Link As urban areas around the world expand, the problem of light pollution will only continue to get worse. The City of Wichita estimates the current population of the Wichita Metropolitan Statistical Area to be over 790,000, and predicts it to grow to over 870,000 by 2035 ( "Demographics" ). With that in mind, the City of Wichita, going forward, should implement strategies to reduce the impact of light pollution on its people and the environment. Causes of Light Pollution # While some loss of light into the sky is unpreventable and is to be expected, inefficient lighting practices and poor lighting design exacerbate the problem by unnecessarily allowing large amounts of light to be wasted into the night sky, where it will not be used. DarkSky International notes several common sources of light pollution. Unshielded Lighting # Many outdoor light fixtures and street lights are designed inefficiently, allowing a significant amount of the light they produce to be emitted in directions where it will never be used, such as directly into the sky. Such light fixtures are described as unshielded , and are one major contributor to light pollution ( "Causes" ). Figure 2: Unshielded street lighting. Image source: By Jonn Leffmann, CC BY 3.0 , Link Electronic Messaging Centers # Modern electronic messaging systems, or electronic billboards, are another major source of light pollution. Combined with their increased brightness over traditionally-illuminated billboards, their inability to be effectively shielded allows them to radiate significant abounts of light into the night sky ( "Causes" ). Figure 3: Electronic Messaging Centers. Image source: By Helena Lopes, Link Unused Light Fixtures Left Running # Since light pollution is simply the result of artificial light being scattered into the atmosphere, any amount of artificial light contributes to light pollution. Through light reflected off objects, even properly shielded light fixtures contribute to light pollution when left illumminated while not in use. Figure 5 shows an almost empty parking lot illuminated with properly shielded light fixtures. Even with the shielding, the parking lot surface still reflects a significant amount of light into the sky. Figure 4: Empty parking lot reflecting light from above back into the sky. Image source: By Allen Versfield, CC BY 4.0 , Link Light fixtures which are brighter than necessary for their intended use case are another contributor to light pollution.

docs.text: While the effects of light pollution on astronomical observations are probably the most obvious and well-known, its effects do not stop there. Research has shown that light pollution has a range of wide-reaching consequences on the lives of people, animals, and even plants. Effects on Astronomy # The effect of light pollution on astronomical observations is probably the most obvious of its effects, and the first most people recognize. Just as atmospheric scattering of sunlight obscures celestial objects during the day, atmospheric scattering of artificial light obscures celestial objects during the night. In recent years, as light emitting diode (LED) fixtures and street lighting has become much more widely adopted, this aspect of light pollution has become even more severe. Most LEDs used in outdoor lighting applications emit large amounts of blue light, which is scattered by the earth’s atmosphere much more effectively than light of longer wavelengths, resulting in even higher levels of light pollution. Effects on People # While they are not as obvious or easily recognized, light pollution also causes several negative effects on the human body. Cardiovascular Health and Metabolism # Multiple physiological processes of the human body are timed by a biological clock, called the circadian rhythm. The circadian rhythm has a period of approximately, but not exactly, 24 hours. To synchronize the circadian rhythm with the 24-hour day, the body requires external input in the form of light entering the eyes. Randy J. Nelson of West Virginia University and Souhad Chbeir of Ohio State University conducted a study that showed how disruption of the circadian rhythm by light pollution results in disruption of other physiological processes controlled by the circadian rhythm, such as metabolism. The result of this, as they showed through citing other studies conducted on night shift workers, is an increased likelihood of being overweight or obese ( Nelson and Chbeir ). Another effect of light pollution, closely related to that of metabolic disruption, is increased risk of cardiovascular disease. In their study, researchers from the Jagiellonian University Medical College and the Johannes Gutenburg University present evidence that suggests an association between exposure to light pollution and "development of cardiovascular risk factors, including hypertension, obesity, diabetes, and atherosclerosis, as well as overt cardiovascular disease" ( Wojciechowska et al. ). Mental Health # Exposure to light pollution has also been shown to have effects on peoples’ mental health. A study published in the academic journal Environmental Sciences Europe discovered a trend between increasing levels of light pollution and increasing rates of anxiety ( Wei et al. ). Additionally, in their study, researchers of the Hebei Medical University in China present evidence that suggests an association between exposure to light pollution and increased risk of depression ( Li et al. ). Effects on the Environment # Before the invention of electric lighting, the plants and animals of the earth lived under night skies free of light pollution. The change to the environment that light pollution brings forces many species of plant and animal life to adapt. However, not every species is as hardy and adaptable as another might be. Effects on Animal Life # One example of animal species affected by light pollution is the Fall Armyworm moth. Yi Ji and a group of researchers from the Nanjing Agricultural University and the University of Konstanz performed a study on this species of moth, which migrates during the night. They subjected the moths to a variety of simulated skyglow gradients of varying direction, and observed that the orientation and direction of the moths was consistently toward the darker region of the gradient, and potentially in a direction contrary to that of their migration route ( Ji et al. ). The Phaedon Cochleariae beetle is another example of animal species affected by light pollution. Sandra Regina Lang and a team of researchers from the Bielefeld University performed a study on this species of beetle, where they subjected the beetles to artificial light of various intensities and durations. Their study revealed that the beetles subjected to the most artificial light exhibited delayed growth and development, increasing mortality and chance of predation. The beetles exposed to the most artificial light also exhibited altered surface chemical profiles, potentially inhibiting communication among individuals ( Lang et al. ). Anther example of animal species affected by light pollution is the Passer domesticus (house sparrow). DiDiAlice Coker and a group of researchers from the University of Nevada, Reno performed a study on this species of sparrow, observing their activity and behavior under three levels of intensity of light pollution. They observed that the sparrows exposed to the highest level of artificial light exhibited increased daily activity, increased activity and restlessness at night, as well as lower rates of feeding offspring ( Coker et al. ). Effects on Plant Life # Plants rely on photosynthesis, a process driven by light, to generate their own food, so it is unsurprising that plants are also affected by light pollution. One example of plant species affected by light pollution is eggplant (Solanum melongena). N. Agrawal and a small group of researchers from the University of Delhi performed a study on this plant species, observing their growth and development under conditions of natural sunlight followed by complete darkness, and conditions of natural sunlight followed by artificial lighting. They discovered that the plants which had grown under conditions receiving artificial light at night possessed significantly altered structure on both the macroscopic and microscopic level. Plants receiving artificial light at night exhibited significant growth of roots, shoots, and leaves, compared to plants not receiving artificial light at night. However, they also were observed to exhibit lower chlorophyll levels and photosynthetic rates, as well as a significant changes in quantities of important minerals. Significant damage to cellular membranes and organelles was also observed ( Agrawal et al. ). Other examples of plant species affected by light pollution are soybean and cannabis. Madigan Eckels and Bruce Bugbee of Utah State University performed a study on these plant species. Their findings demonstrated a connection between exposure to artificial light at night and delayed flower growth and increased vertical growth ( Eckels and Bugbee ). Another plant species affected by light pollution is Erythrostemon gilliesii. Julieta Belén Bariles and a small team of researchers from the National University of Córdoba in Argentina performed a study on this plant species, where they observed its pollination under various levels of light pollution and tree cover. Their observations showed that plants in an environment of high light pollution received the least pollen, while plants in an environment of low light pollution tended to receive more pollen ( Bariles et al. ). Effects on the Economy # Light pollution is the result of light lost into the night sky. This wasted light results in increased energy usage, which, in turn, results in increased energy costs.

docs.text: As light pollution is simply the result of artificial light being wasted into the night sky, the strategies that should be implemented to reduce the amount of light pollution are quite straightforward. DarkSky International lists several strategies to reduce wasted light that contributes to light pollution. Figure 1: Several effective strategies to reduce light pollution. Image source: Link Outdoor lighting should be installed only where it will be needed and used ( "Principles" ). Light that goes unused simply ends up reflected into the sky and wasted. Outdoor light fixtures should be fully shielded to direct light only where it is necessary and will be useful ( "Principles" ). Unshielded light fixtures emit light in directions where it is not needed, resulting in glare and skyglow. Light fixtures should emit only the minimum amount of light necessary to accomplish their task ( "Principles" ). Operation of lights that are brighter than necessary will result in more light reflected into the sky, increasing light pollution. Outdoor lighting should be powered off when not in use, through the use of timers and/or motion sensors ( "Principles" ). As previously mentioned, unused light ends up wasted into the sky. Because warmer colored light is not as strongly scattered by the atmosphere as cooler colored light is, warmer colored lamps should be used in outdoor light fixtures ( "Principles" ). Figure 2: Fully shielded light fixture. Image source: By Allen Versfield, CC BY 4.0 , Link Implementation in Wichita # The City of Wichita has been growing, and is expected to continue growing. As previously mentioned, the City of Wichita estimates the population of the Wichita Metropolitan Statistical Area to be in excess of 790,000, and expects it to grow to over 870,000 by 2035 ( "Demographics" ). This is illustrated in Figure 3, which shows a map of the Wichita area with light pollution data overlaid. Larger increases in light pollution between 2013 and 2024 are indicated by warmer colors, which cover much of the outskirts of Wichita. This is reflective of an expanding population. Figure 3: The change in light pollution in Wichita, KS, between 2013 and 2024. Warmer colors indicate larger increases in light pollution. Image source: Link The City of Wichita should invest in implementing the strategies outlined above, to reduce light pollution, and to benefit both local and surrounding communities, as well as the environment. Such investment will also yield returns in long-term energy savings. DarkSky International reports that the city of Tucson, Arizona, which has implemented these strategies, has seen annual energy savings of millions of dollars ( "Nights over Tucson" ). Common Misconception # Some may argue that bright outdoor lighting is necessary to ensure a safe environment for people at night. However, as DarkSky International points out, bright, unshielded outdoor lighting causes glare, reducing one’s night vision, and obscuring areas in shadow. A survey conducted in Melbourne revealed that many women identified brightly-lit areas as less safe. Additionally, studies have shown that less lighting results in a safer environment. For example, a study was performed in England and Wales, where the streetlights were dimmed and powered off completely, yet no increase in traffic accidents or criminal activity was recorded. Another study was conducted in Chicago, where a 21% increase in criminal activity in the experimental area was recorded following installation of brighter light fixtures ( "Reduce Crime" ). Conclusion # At first thought, light pollution may seem to be an issue only for the astronomy community. However, the actual effects it has on people and the environment, and the waste of money associated with it, should not be ignored. By taking action in implementing strategies to reduce light pollution, the City of Wichita will not only save energy costs in the long term, but will also lead the way in improving the health of the community and the environment, and in making the night sky more accessible to the people of the Wichita area.
